body:
Note: If you used #107722 as a base, you should list @Lazy-Rabbit-2001 as a co-author.

---

> You would still want a `@final` annotation even in a non-virtual-by-default model. Hence this opinion has no impact on this change.

I disagree with this. If you take the approach of "non-static methods are non-virtual by default" (even if technically they aren't), there is no point in using `@final` on methods. You are relying on GDScript to produce a warning/error when overriding a "non-virtual" method. That's your goal: not to use `@final` on every method. There is no point in further restricting something that should already be restricted.

If you take the approach of "non-static methods are virtual by default" (which they technically are), there is no point in marking a virtual method as `@virtual`. It's a tautology.

So I still think `@virtual` and `@final` on methods are not very compatible. We could add them both, so that users can use whichever they prefer. But this is not very good from a language design and project consistency perspective, both annotations should not be used simultaneously in the same project (and it's even worse considering that addons and libraries may follow a different style).

> Further on that note, GDS already has virtual-by-default semantics **as a core language feature**. Changing that, at this point in the language, is a non-starter.

I don't argue that we can't change this in 4.x for compatibility reasons. But I think we could use warnings to introduce `@virtual` and `@override` instead of `@final` for methods in a non-breaking manner.

> Note: If you used https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/107722 as a base, you should list @Lazy-Rabbit-2001 as a co-author.

Yep, my bad. I'm not used to doing that for other projects - I think it's a bit late to try and add the co-author marker to the commits unless you think I should rewrite the commit history. Otherwise I'm not sure where else to note it. Somewhere in the PR body?

> there is no point in using `@final` on methods.

The point of a `@final` marker is to state, at some point in a virtual inheritance tree, that the inheritance _must stop_. This is the reason why C++ has simultaneous `virtual`, `override`, and `final` markers, even with a non-virtual-by-default model.

I think your disagreement with it is really a disagreement with the current virtual-by-default model. I would want `@final` to be present _regardless_ of the model used, and I think discussion about the model is exceptionally out of scope of this feature.

> So I still think `@virtual` and `@final` on methods are not very compatible.

I think this still continues to assume that `@final` _existing_ implies "virtual-by-default", which is not true. Imagine a non-virtual-by-default model with `@virtual`, `@override,` and `@final` markers. Those permit us to express the following constructs:

```gdscript
class_name A

@virtual func foo() -> void:
    pass

func bar() -> void:
    pass
    
@virtual func foobar() -> void:
    pass


class B extends A

# Legal. @final implies @override and @virtual
# Children will not be able to change the behavior of this method.
@final func foo() -> void:
    pass

# Error. Since `A::bar()` is non-virtual, we can't `@override` it or otherwise treat it as a virtual function.
# Using either `@override` or `@virtual` will fail here since we cannot "upgrade" a method to virtual.
@override func bar() -> void:
    pass

# Legal. @override implies @virtual 
# Children can still change the behavior of this method.
@override func foobar() -> void:
    pass
    
class C extends B

# Error. B (the superclass) has declared this virtual method (originally from A) as `@final`.
@override func foo() -> void:
    pass

# This is an interesting case. In the current model (virtual-by-default) this is an implicit `@override`.
# In a non-virtual-by-default model, we have two options:
# 1. This is an error due to reuse of the function name `bar` (which is most consistent).
# 2. This is legal, and this non-virtual function _shadows_ `A::bar()` when being invoked directly on a statically-typed C instance.
# C++ uses (2), but I don't think something like (2) is implementable given current GDS architecture.
func bar() -> void:
    pass

# Legal. Following expected behavior, we can keep overriding non-final virtual functions.
@override func foobar() -> void:
    pass
```

I (and others) would still want to be able to use `@final` in a non-virtual-by-default model in the exact same manner that it is used in the current virtual-by-default model.

> I'm not used to doing that for other projects - I think it's a bit late to try and add the co-author marker to the commits unless you think I should rewrite the commit history.

Yes, you can and should rewrite the commit history of feature branchs. As long as the PR is not merged, it does not violate anyone's expectations. So you should squash all commits into one, add `Co-authored-by: Author <email>` to the commit message, and force push the branch in your fork.

In this project, PRs usually have a single commit (except in rare cases where it is more convenient to split a large amount of changes into several independent and self-contained commits). Authors often force push every time they make a change to a PR, instead of making many small commits and then squashing them.

---

> ```gdscript
> # Legal. @final implies @override and @virtual
> # Children will not be able to change the behavior of this method.
> @final func foo() -> void:
>     pass
> ```

You are introducing a new definition (`@final = @virtual + @override`) that is not obvious, not widely used, and does not make sense for methods that are initially defined as non-virtual (in the model "virtual by default").

I don't think it's necessary to explicitly declare a virtual method final in the model "non-virtual by default". If you use `@override func foo()`, you are declaring a final (non-virtual) overriding method. If you use `@virtual @override func foo()`, you are defining a virtual overriding method (which can again be overridden in descendants of class `B`).

Also, I don't really like the method shadowing feature that C++ has. I understand why it was done, but I think that name shadowing is a recipe for subtle and hard-to-debug issues. I would prefer that methods that are declared non-virtual (either original methods or overrides) could no longer be overridden in descendant classes.

So my opinion hasn't changed, even after your demonstration.

> > So a final class that extends from Node should not be attachable to Node2D IMO
> 
> I don't know enough about GD's serialization to comment on this effectively. I'm not sure I follow how this would improve the security of serialization.

This is not specific about current builtin GD serialization. It is about guarantees that are needed to implement secure serialization.

Basically if you save some object of class `A` and want to load an instance of `A` later, it is not only necessary to save all the properties of `A`. You also need a solution for polymorphism since the object might be of a type `B` that inherits `A`. Solving this can be quite complex to do in a save way, especially in a context where scripts can be dynamically loaded (e.g. `B` is loaded from a resource pack). To solve this Godot just stores the script path and loads the script when de-serializing. This solves the polymorphism problem but allows loading arbitrary scripts which is not good for certain use cases.

This is where final classes become interesting since they can provide a guarantee that the object can not be of an inherited type. So serialization does not need polymorphism solutions, it is enough to serialize the properties.

But that isn't really true since Godot has no "straight" inheritance chain for objects. An object has a native type (the builtin types or GDExtension types). And a script can be attached to an object. When you write `extends Node` in GDScript it means that the GDScript can be attached to objects wich have `Node` or a subtype as the native type.

So when you write `@final extends Node` you might not be able to inherit the script. But if you are still able to attach the script to subtypes of `Node`, the above guarantee does not apply and you still need to account for polymorphism even when dealing with final classes since the native type of the object might vary.

> 2\. `@final` is only usable on _named_ classes (and not script files).

As someone who tries to avoid polluting the global scope as much as possible, that is kinda a deal breaker for me. Is there a good reason for this limitation?

> You are introducing a new definition (`@final = @virtual + @override`) that is not obvious, not widely used, and does not make sense

I don't think that's a fair statement. That is how `final` works in C++. `final` implies `override` and `override` implies `virtual`.

> I don't think it's necessary to explicitly declare a virtual method final in the model "non-virtual by default".

That might be what we're disagreeing on here. Let me formalize both of our definitions and see if we can come to a consensus:

My operating definitions are:
* `virtual` - Marks a _method hierarchy_ as being virtual. Calls to these methods must use virtual dispatch. Must only be applied by the top-level declaration in the hierarchy.
* `override` - In a _virtual hierarchy_, defines that a method must override a superclass method. Not usable in a non-virtual hierarchy.
* `final` - In a _virtual hierarchy_, defines that a method that is overriding a parent method may not further be overridden by subclasses.

It seems that your operating definitions are:
* `virtual` - Marks a _single method_ as virtual. Methods without this marker may not be replicated in a subclass.
* `override` - Defines that a method must override a superclass method. Not usable unless the immediate method being overridden is `virtual`.
* `final` - Theoretically not relevant. `override` does not imply `virtual` and thus this marker is not needed for methods.

The difference being that I am working on the basis that `virtual` is a property of a hierarchy and you are working on the basis that `virtual` is a property of an individual method.

The _common case_ for virtual function overrides is to override the method and continue to permit further overrides. In your model, that would make the common case `@virtual @override func ...`. I think this is too cumbersome a burden to place here. 

Your model also relies on _implicit finality_. That is, absence of `@virtual` implies `@final`, rather than explicit finality. That deviates from how `@final` would be used in classes (which is not great for consistency), and deviates from how virtual method hierarchies work in other languages that users will be familiar with (C++, C#, Java).

Given the current model is virtual-by-default (and I do not see this changing due to it being a **major** break), I think introduction of `@final` in the _current fashion_ is the best solution. If we elect to revisit the virtual-by-default status at some point in the future (GDScript 3.0), we can tweak the semantics.

I was thinking about it a bit further, and the combo of `virtual` / `override` / `final` allows us to concisely describe virtual method hierarchies in simple terms.

`virtual` - I want to _declare_ a virtual hierarchy.
`override` - I want to _continue_ a virtual hierarchy.
`final` - I want to _end_ a virtual hierarchy.

It's a solid single-keyword solution for dealing with it.

___

And then back to serialization - 

> loads the script when de-serializing

_oh no_. I'm getting Java serialization flashbacks from reading that. While dispatch in serialization will always be necessary, that mechanism is a RCE nightmare. "not good for certain use cases" is putting it lightly.

> When you write extends Node in GDScript it means that the GDScript can be attached to objects wich have Node or a subtype as the native type.

That's... _weird_, to say the least. I guess it sounds useful if you want to reuse a script, but it doesn't really sound like the right solution for things. I would expect the script-type of an object and the runtime type of an object to actually match, not for the script-type to be implicitly promoted when using a script of a disjoint supertype.

Is that a commonly used feature? It seems weird to make an exception here for `@final` types, and it would make more sense to disallow this behavior entirely.

> So when you write `@final extends Node` you might not be able to inherit the script.
> ...
> Is there a good reason for this limitation?

Those two sort of tie together - are you even able to inherit from a script without a `class_name`? The script is not addressable as it has no name, so you can't target it with `extends`. 

Unless there's some magic syntax I'm unaware of, this property makes it _implicitly_ `final` and thus there is no point to permit explicit `@final` markers on anonymous scripts.

> Those two sort of tie together - are you even able to inherit from a script without a `class_name`? The script is not addressable as it has no name, so you can't target it with `extends`. 

```gdscript
# Extends from an anonymous script class
extends "res://dir/my_script.gd"
```

In Godot every script file is born as a class but anonymous.

Ah well that's terrifying. I guess that's what happens without namespaces/packages. I've never actually encountered that syntax.

Alright, well, `@final` scripts it is. I think the other points still hold.

> Is that a commonly used feature? It seems weird to make an exception here for `@final` types, and it would make more sense to disallow this behavior entirely.

I recall suggesting this once, but apparently quite a lot of people use it for utility scripts.

Huh. I wonder why that is. Maybe due to lack of other language features that make reusing scripts easy (traits or similar)? IMO this would be better addressed by not making an exception for `@final` and changing how the behavior of "attaching a script to a subtyped node" works.

If we adopted a model where attaching a script to a subtyped node makes an "instanced" script (effectively an invisible clone that updates when the parent updates, similar to an inherited scene) where the type is upgraded `Node -> Node2D` (though this might not work with named classes, which continues to make me think this whole feature is pretty weird), then those "instanced" scripts can provide sane serialization semantics.

I would consider that out of scope for this change though. We should cement `@final` with a design and then address the co-opting of scripts and their impacts on serialization.

> I would consider that out of scope for this change though. We should cement `@final` with a design and then address the co-opting of scripts and their impacts on serialization.

I highly disagree. Lifting such a limitation in the future is no problem, but adding it at a later point is basically impossible due to compatibility.

As long as we don't have this figured out we should add the feature in a more limited scope, that is easy to expand.

As far as I can tell, adding the restriction on serialization is going to require making core aware of final classes. I started looking into doing that, but it seems a much larger change than this GDS-specific change here. I'm also not sure where the API/ABI boundary lies for core to determine if that will be a breaking change.

Okay, updated to be able to attach to anon scripts and to have the attachment restriction in place for `@final` scripts.
@HolonProduction @dalexeev any other outstanding concerns?
